At dusk the drovers rinsed their tin cups in the overflow trough before dipping from the center, and each morning the basin stood clear again, reflecting the first pale strip of sky.

After an autumn dust-blow left red silt on the bottom step, the mason hung a woven reed lattice across the south gap and began asking each traveler where they had slept the night before before lifting the latch.

At daybreak the stone bakehouse by the pier stood open to the salt wind, and wet deckhands shared warm rye loaves beside the brick oven.

By November the clerk bolted an iron shutter across the oven window and demanded a stamped copper tally before anyone could stand near the heat, leaving shivering net-menders outside on the sleet-slick planks.
Outside, frozen boots shuffled past the shuttered brickwork in the sleet; inside the quiet room, the baker brushed a single pinch of flour from his apron and aligned the brass weights on the shelf.

When the overheated flue latch finally snapped and flung the iron shutter wide, warm cedar smoke and fresh loaves poured onto the wharf; the shivering net-menders gathered close to eat while the baker sat quietly by the open threshold.
